rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tafsir began in the Prophet’s lifetime, when companions asked about Quranic meanings; later leading interpreters included Ali, Ibn Abbas, Zayd, Ubayy, Ibn Masud, and Abdullah ibn Amr.
rows.anchor: قد سأل عن بعض معاني القرآن كما سأله عمر رضي الله عنه عن الكلالة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tafsir spread as non-Arab converts needed the Quran explained, and Ibn Ashur regards it as the noblest and foremost Islamic science.
rows.anchor: حين دخل في الإسلام من لم يكن عربي السجية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj of Mecca (80–149 AH) was the first to compile tafsir, covering many verses and gathering reports, especially from Ibn Abbas’s students Ata and Mujahid.
rows.anchor: أول من صنف فيه عبد الملك بن جريج المكي المولود سنة 80 ه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The tafsir of Ibn Abbas transmitted through Muhammad al-Kalbi from Abu Salih was criticized; Abu Salih was accused of lying, making this one of the weakest transmissions.
rows.anchor: وقد رمي أبو صالح بالكذب حتى لقب بكلمة دروغدت بالفارسية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adding Muhammad ibn Marwan al-Suddi’s route through al-Kalbi was called a chain of lies, contrasted with the so-called golden chain of Malik, Nafi, and Ibn Umar.
rows.anchor: فإذا انضم إليها رواية محمد بن مروان السدى عن الكلبي فهي سلسلة الكذب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It was alleged that al-Kalbi was associated with Abdullah ibn Saba, who promoted extreme claims about Ali, including that Ali had not died and would return.
rows.anchor: الكلبي كان من أصحاب عبد الله بن سبأ اليهودي الأصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Among reports attributed to Ibn Abbas from Muqatil, al-Dahhak, and Ali ibn Abi Talha, Ibn Ashur considers Ali ibn Abi Talha’s the soundest; al-Bukhari relied on it for glosses.
rows.anchor: وأصحها رواية علي بن أبي طلحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fabricators and obscuring transmitters used Ibn Abbas’s fame as cover to authenticate reports they circulated.
rows.anchor: قد اتخذها الوضاعون والمدلسون ملجأ لتصحيح ما يروونه

rows.speaker: أبو جحيفة
rows.claim: Abu Juhaifa asked Ali whether the family possessed revelation beyond the Quran; Ali swore they did not, except for understanding God grants a person of the Quran.
rows.anchor: عن أبي جحيفة قال : قلت لعلي هل عندكم شيء من الوحي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most tafsir reports ascribed to Ali are fabricated, except those with sound chains; Ibn Ashur cites the Abu Juhaifa report as evidence of Ali’s Quranic understanding.
rows.anchor: وهنالك روايات تسند لعلي رضي الله عنه ، أكثرها من الموضوعات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Later Quran commentators followed different approaches and intellectual tastes.
rows.anchor: ثم تلاحق العلماء في تفسير القرآن وسلك كل فريق مسلكا يأوي إليه وذوقا يعتمد عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The transmitted-report approach is associated first with Malik and also al-Dawudi; al-Tabari is its best-known representative in the available works.
rows.anchor: وأشهر أهل هذه الطريقة فيما هو بأيدي الناس محمد بن جرير الطبري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some commentators used reasoned analysis, while many relied heavily on Israelite stories, causing fabricated material to proliferate in their books.
rows.anchor: وشغف كثير بنقل القصص عن الإسرائيليات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya both probe meanings, cite Arabic evidence and earlier exegetes; rhetoric and Arabic predominate for al-Zamakhshari, while law predominates for Ibn Atiyya, and both became major references.
rows.anchor: يأتي بشواهدها من كلام العرب ويذكر كلام المفسرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet fixed the order of Quranic verses according to revelation, and that distinctive arrangement contributes to the Quran’s inimitability.
rows.anchor: فلم تختلف قراءة النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم في ترتيب آي السور على نحو ما هو في المصحف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reordering verses within a sura would destroy the inimitable style; the Prophet’s recitation followed the arrangement preserved in the present codex and confirmed in the final review.
rows.anchor: لو غير عنه إلى ترتيب آخر لنزل على حد الإعجاز الذي امتاز به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The arrangement was transmitted by companion memorizers from the Prophet’s final recitations; Zayd did not depart from it when compiling the codex for Abu Bakr.
rows.anchor: استقرت عليه رواية الحفاظ من الصحابة عن العرضات الأخيرة التي كان يقرأ بها النبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muslims preserved the Quran chiefly through memorized recitation in prayers and other occasions; scribes wrote revelations on the Prophet’s command, and writing may have been intended as recourse in case of doubt or forgetting.
rows.anchor: حفظ القرآن كل من حفظه كلا أو بعضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The companions are not reported to have disputed the order of any sura’s verses or objected to the collected Quran; it matched their memorization.
rows.anchor: لم يؤثر عنهم أنهم فرددوا في ترتيب آيات من إحدى السور ولا أثر عنهم إنكار أو اختلاف

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Ibn Wahb reports hearing Malik say that the Quran was arranged in the order in which people heard it from the Messenger of God.
rows.anchor: سمعت مالكا يقول : إنما ألف القرآن على ما كانوا يسمعونه

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbari says Gabriel showed the Prophet where a verse belonged, including verses revealed in response to a question; the arrangement of letters, verses, and suras came from the Messenger.
rows.anchor: كانت الآية تنزل جوابا لمستخبر يسأل ويوقف جبريل رسول الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Normally, a verse relates to the one after it through a shared purpose, transition, or another form of connected discourse.
rows.anchor: فلهذا كان الأصل في آي القرآن أن يكون بين الآية ولاحقتها تناسب في الغرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Conjunctions such as fa, lakin, and bal, and exception particles, signal connection but do not prove that adjacent passages were revealed in that order.
rows.anchor: على أن وجود ذلك لا يعين اتصال ما بعده بما قبله في النزول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase “except those with an excuse” in 4:95 was agreed to have been revealed after the surrounding text, showing that textual connection does not establish revelation sequence.
rows.anchor: قوله تعالى ) غير أولي الضرر ( نزل بعد نزول ما قبله

rows.speaker: بعض مشايخنا المحققين
rows.claim: A verified teacher of al-Zarkashi rejects the claim that one should not seek verse connections: first ask whether each verse completes the previous one or stands independently, then seek its relation.
rows.anchor: قال بدر الدين الزركشي بعض مشايخنا المحققين قد وهم من قال لا تطلب للآي الكريمة مناسبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gabriel reportedly paused revelation for days; after he resumed with the preceding verses of Mary, the Prophet reproached him and God directed him to answer with 19:64.
rows.anchor: جبريل لبث أياما لم ينزل على النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم بوحي

rows.speaker: عمر
rows.claim: Umar urged people to consult their poetic canon, saying Arab poetry contains interpretations of scripture and meanings of speech.
rows.anchor: فقال عمر عليكم بديوانكم لا تضلوا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas calls poetry the Arabs’ register and says obscure Quranic vocabulary should be clarified from their poetry, which he often recited when asked.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس الشعر ديوان العرب فإذا خفي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: As quoted by al-Qurtubi, Ibn Abbas explained “sina” in 2:255 as drowsiness and cited Zuhayr’s verse as evidence for the word’s sense.
rows.anchor: قال القرطبي سئل ابن عباس

rows.speaker: زهير
rows.claim: Zuhayr’s line is cited as poetic evidence that سنة means drowsiness or sleepiness.
rows.anchor: قول زهير : لا سنة في طوال الليل تأخذه

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Ikrima explained zanīm as an illegitimate child and cited a poem as evidence.
rows.anchor: وسئل عكرمة ما معنى الزنيم ، فقال هو ولد الزنى

rows.speaker: أحمد بن حنبل
rows.claim: Ahmad ibn Hanbal reportedly said he disliked a person’s use of a poetic line to explain Quranic meaning; Ibn Ashur calls the reported response puzzling.
rows.anchor: فمما يؤثر عن أحمد بن حنبل رحمه الله ، أنه سئل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If Ahmad’s disapproval is authentic, Ibn Ashur thinks he likely objected to using poetry to challenge the soundness of Quranic wording, as some unbelievers did.
rows.anchor: لعله يريد كراهة أن يذكر الشعر لإثبات صحة ألفاظ القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn al-Rawandi challenged Ibn al-Aʿrabi over whether “garment of piety” was Arabic; Ibn al-Aʿrabi answered with a pun denying that he lacked mastery of Arabic.
rows.anchor: قال لابن الأعرابي : أتقول العرب لباس التقوى

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: Aisha told the young Urwa that the Safa–Marwa verse was revealed about Ansar who had worshipped at Manat near Qudayd and hesitated to perform the rite after becoming Muslim.
rows.anchor: إنما نزلت هذه الآية في الأنصار

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: Aisha corrected Urwa’s inference that “no blame” made the Safa–Marwa rite optional: if abstention were intended, the verse would say there is no blame in not performing it.
rows.anchor: كلا لو كان كما تقول ، لكانت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prophetic explanations of Quran are few; Ibn Atiyya’s report from Aisha that the Prophet explained only a limited number concerns unseen matters and generalities requiring revelation.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية عن عائشة ما كان رسول الله يفسر من القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some prophetic explanations did not require revelation: the Prophet told Adi ibn Hatim that the white and black threads mean daylight and night, and joked that his pillow was broad.
rows.anchor: كما بين لعدي بن حاتم أن الخيط الأبيض والخيط الأسود هما سواد الليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports from companions who witnessed revelation identify those who incurred wrath as Jews and those astray as Christians.
rows.anchor: المراد من ) المغضوب عليهم ( اليهود ومن ) الضالين ( النصارى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The transmitted referent of “leave me with the one I created alone” is al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, father of Khalid ibn al-Walid.
rows.anchor: الوليد بن المغيرة المخزومي أبا خالد بن الوليد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The referent in 19:77 is al-As ibn Waʾil in his dispute with Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, as reported in al-Bukhari’s tafsir of al-Muddaththir.
rows.anchor: العاصي بن وائل السهمي في خصومته بينه وبين خباب بن الأرت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran chooses apt Arabic words that convey all intended meanings in context, whether literal or figurative; contextual clues guide any shift in sense.
rows.anchor: لا يوجد في كلمات القرآن كلمة تقصر دلالتها عن جميع المقصود منها في حالة تركيبها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In 68:25, the word ḥard is chosen so that all its meanings can serve the intended purpose.
rows.anchor: إيثار كلمة حرد في قوله تعالى ) وغدوا على حرد قادرين (

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb أتوا in 25:40 incorporates the meaning of مروا, allowing it to take على; the wording evokes both reaching the town and passing by it to reflect on its people’s fate.
rows.anchor: فجاء فعل أتوا مضمنا معنى مروا فعدي بحرف على

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Such semantic and syntactic choices are fine points of eloquent speech, rarely matched by human rhetoricians because human intelligence cannot encompass all their subtleties.
rows.anchor: فإن اقتضى الحال تصرفا في معنى اللفظ كان التصرف بطريق التضمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second, often overlooked aspect of eloquence is the Quran’s innovative variety of rhetorical styles, with forms suited to different aims and modes of expression.
rows.anchor: وأما الجهة الثانية وهى ما أبدعه القرآن من أفانين التصرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arab literary expression comprised poetry and prose; prose included sermons and soothsayers’ rhymed speech, while writers and poets often repeated inherited forms.
rows.anchor: والنثر خطابة وأسجاع كهان ، وأصحاب هذه الأنواع وإن تنافسوا في ابتكار المعاني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeated openings and parallel lines show how poets imitated established forms; Imruʾ al-Qays’s line in his Muʿallaqa is echoed by Tarafa with the rhyme word changed to وتجلد.
rows.anchor: وقوفا بها صحبي على مطيهم يقولون لا تهلك أسى وتحمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surviving speeches of Suḥban and Quss ibn Saʿida suggest that Arab oratory also shared a narrow, uniform style; soothsayer rhymes used short clauses and rare words.
rows.anchor: وكذلك القول في خطبهم تكاد تكون لهجة واحدة وأسلوبا واحدا فيما بلغنا من خطب سحبان وقس بن ساعدة

rows.speaker: عمر
rows.claim: Umar described poetry as the people’s knowledge and their soundest knowledge, reflecting poetry’s dominance in their eloquent competition.
rows.anchor: قال عمر كان الشعر علم القوم ولم يكن لهم علم أصح منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran was neither poetry nor soothsayer rhyme but closer to sermons; it introduced many styles and gives Arabic speakers varied forms suited to their purposes.
rows.anchor: فلما جاء القرآن ولم يكن شعرا ولا سجع كهان

rows.speaker: الوليد بن المغيرة
rows.claim: After hearing the Prophet recite, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira said the Quran was neither a soothsayer’s chant nor poetry, despite his familiarity with poetic meters.
rows.anchor: قال الوليد ابن المغيرة لما استمع إلى قراءة النبي

rows.speaker: أنيس بن جنادة الغفاري
rows.claim: Unays ibn Junada al-Ghifari told Abu Dharr that the Prophet’s words were unlike soothsayer speech and did not fit poetic meters; Unays later became Muslim.
rows.anchor: وصفه أنيس بن جنادة الغفاري الشاعر أخو أبي ذر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Similar descriptions of the Quran as neither soothsayer speech nor poetry are attributed to Utba ibn Rabiʿa and al-Nadr ibn al-Harith.
rows.anchor: وورد مثل هذه الصفة عن عتبة بن ربيعة والنضر بن الحرث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Ashur says opponents called the Quran poetry as a concession to familiar prestigious speech, since its subtle meanings, ordered construction, and power over minds were evident.
rows.anchor: ألحقوه بأشبه الكلام به فقالوا إنه شعر تقريبا للدهماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the Quran is extensive prose with varied subjects, its style is smooth, consistent in eloquence, and easier to memorize than poetry.
rows.anchor: أسلوبه يجري على الألسنة سلسا سهلا لا تفاوت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Meter helped Arabs preserve poetry by balancing words and making them flow easily; even leading poets differ in fluency and are excused for poetic licenses.
rows.anchor: لأن ما يقتضيه من الوزن يلجئ إلى التدريب على ألفاظ متوازنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Exegetes often searched for occasions of revelation, events said to prompt a verse to explain a ruling, narrate an event, condemn it, or serve another purpose.
rows.anchor: وهي حوادث يروى أن آيات من القرآن نزلت لأجلها لبيان حكمها أو لحكايتها أو إنكارها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some exegetes overdid this search until readers could think every Quranic verse descended in response to a particular event, weakening confidence in their accounts.
rows.anchor: وأغربوا في ذلك وأكثروا حتى كاد بعضهم أن يوهم الناس أن كل آية من القرآن نزلت على سبب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some verses themselves point to their occasion, and some occasions are established through transmission rather than a narrator’s conjecture; ignoring the topic entirely also risks misunderstanding.
rows.anchor: نجد في بعض آي القرآن إشارة إلى الأسباب التي دعت إلى نزولها ونجد لبعض الآي أسبابا ثبتت بالنقل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Ashur discusses occasions of revelation in his introduction to assess them carefully during exegesis and avoid repeating the methodological discussion.
rows.anchor: فذلك الذي دعاني إلى خوض هذا الغرض في مقدمات التفسير لظهور شدة الحاجة إلى تمحيصه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He excuses early authors who collected many occasions because enthusiasm for a new subject naturally led them to expand their compilations.
rows.anchor: وأنا عاذر المتقدمين الذين ألفوا في أسباب النزول فاستكثروا منها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He does not excuse leading exegetes who accepted weak reports without marking their reliability, creating the false impression that revelation depended on triggering events.
rows.anchor: ولكني لا أعذر أساطين المفسرين الذين تلقفوا الروايات الضعيفة فأثبتوها في كتبهم ولم ينبهوا على مراتبها قوة وضعفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran guides people toward communal well-being and does not need events to occur before it can reveal legislation.
rows.anchor: فإن القرآن جاء هاديا إلى ما به صلاح الأمة في أصناف الصلاح فلا يتوقف نزوله على حدوث الحوادث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most scholars say an occasion of revelation does not restrict a verse’s general wording; a deviant minority claimed that it does.
rows.anchor: إن سبب النزول لا يخصص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The usul principle is that general wording governs rather than the specific occasion, though some reports try to specify general wording or restrict an unrestricted expression and can distort interpretation.
rows.anchor: العبرة بعموم اللفظ لا بخصوص السبب ولكن أسبابا كثيرة رام رواتها تعيين مراد

rows.speaker: الواحدي
rows.claim: Al-Wahidi warns that people now invent occasions of revelation and fabricate lies; he says such claims require reports heard from eyewitnesses of revelation.
rows.anchor: الواحدي في أول كتابه في أسباب النزول

words: ومن لم يحكم بما أنزل الله
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Knowing the occasion of 5:44 clarifies that “whoever” is relative, not conditional: the verse concerns Christians who abandoned the Gospel, so their disbelief in Muhammad is unsurprising.
rows.anchor: ثم إذا علم أن سبب النزول هم النصارى

words: الذين آمنوا ولم يلبسوا إيمانهم بظلم
rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud reports that the companions were distressed by 6:82, taking “injustice” to mean sin, until the Prophet clarified it.
rows.anchor: حديث عبد الله بن مسعود قال لما نزل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet’s clarification identifies the “injustice” in 6:82 with associating partners with God, citing Luqman’s description of shirk as great injustice.
rows.anchor: إنه ليس بذلك ? ألا تسمع لقول لقمان لابنه إن الشرك لظلم عظيم

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: Aisha explained to Urwa that orphan girls under guardians’ care shared their wealth, and guardians wishing to marry them without fair dowers were told to marry other women.
rows.anchor: عن عائشة أن عروة بن الزبير سألها عنها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The occasion of revelation explains the otherwise obscure link in 4:3 between the condition about fairness to orphans and the command to marry other women.
rows.anchor: الملازمة بين الشرط وجزائه فيبينها ما في الصحيح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran guides and legislates for a community through material that may precede need, admonish or praise particular people, or address everyone fit to hear it.
rows.anchor: كتاب جاء لهدي أمة والتشريع لها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quranic legislation and ethical instruction uses broad principles to make religion easy to understand, preserve it through transmission, and give scholars room to derive rulings.
rows.anchor: وقد يكون مخاطبا به جميع من يصلح لخطابه ، وهو في جميع ذلك قد جاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran’s concise form is deliberate; God could have revealed much more or extended the Prophet’s lifetime, and 5:3 declares the completion of divine favor.
rows.anchor: فكما لا يجوز حمل كلماته على خصوصيات جزئية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One must neither narrow general wording that is meant broadly nor generalize wording intended specifically or make a restricted statement absolute, since this confuses or defeats the intended meaning.
rows.anchor: لا يجوز تعميم ما قصد منه الخصوص ولا إطلاق ما قصد منه التقييد

rows.speaker: ابن سيرين
rows.claim: Ibn Sirin says the Kharijites applied threat verses revealed about polytheists to Muslims, producing the innovation of declaring people unbelievers for sin.
rows.anchor: قال ابن سيرين في الخوارج

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: The Haruriyya quoted “judgment belongs only to God” against Ali during arbitration; he replied that it was a true statement used for a false purpose.
rows.anchor: قال الحرورية لعلي رضي الله عنه يوم التحكيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Revelation accompanying events also demonstrates the Quran’s miraculous ability to answer spontaneously and refutes the claim that it is merely ancient tales.
rows.anchor: وثمة فائدة أخرى عظيمة لأسباب النزول وهي أن في نزول القرآن عند حدوث حوادث دلالة على إعجازه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prophetic explanations sometimes draw on a possible sense beyond the construction’s primary meaning, awakening listeners to the full range of meanings Quranic wording can bear.
rows.anchor: أنه ليس هو المعنى الأسبق من التركيب

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد بن المعلى
rows.claim: Abu Saʿid ibn al-Muʿalla reports that the Prophet called him during prayer; after he finished, the Prophet asked why he had not answered and cited 8:24.
rows.anchor: ما رواه أبو سعيد بن المعلى قال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse primarily means obey God and the Messenger, with “call” meaning guidance and “what gives you life” meaning what benefits you; the Prophet also applied the literal sense of answering a call.
rows.anchor: المعنى المسوقة فيه الآية هو الاستجابة بمعنى الامتثال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The resurrection report’s comparison to the first creation primarily counters doubts about resurrection; the Prophet also used it to indicate complete likeness, including being barefoot and unclothed.
rows.anchor: إنما هو تشبيه الخلق الثاني بالخلق الأول لدفع استبعاد البعث

words: استغفر لهم أو لا تستغفر لهم
rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: When Umar objected to praying for the hypocrite Abdullah ibn Ubayy, the Prophet replied that God had given him a choice and he would seek forgiveness more than seventy times.
rows.anchor: لعمر بن الخطاب لما قال له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet took “seek forgiveness or do not” as a real choice, though its apparent rhetorical meaning is equivalence; he also treated seventy as a literal count rather than hyperbole.
rows.anchor: على التخيير مع أن ظاهره أنه مستعمل في التسوية

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: When Umm Kulthum bint ʿUqba migrated to Medina and refused to return to the polytheists, the Prophet recited “He brings the living out of the dead” in a figurative application.
rows.anchor: ومن هذا قول النبي لأم كلثوم بنت عقبة بن معيط حين جاءت مسلمة مهاجرة إلى المدينة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet’s prostrations at Quranic prostration passages may reflect this principle of drawing out a possible meaning; if revealed, they provide stronger evidence that God intends meanings the wording can bear without opposing its aims.
rows.anchor: وما أرى سجود النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم في مواضع سجود التلاوة من القرآن إلا راجعا إلى هذا الأصل
